lead: Text classification maps a document to a label such as spam or not spam. The document first becomes a feature vector, usually word counts or TF-IDF weights. A supervised classifier then learns from labelled examples how those features point to each label. Naive Bayes learns class-conditional word probabilities, logistic regression learns weights for a probability, and a linear SVM learns a separating margin. These methods are fast, need little memory, and run well on a phone. They are used for spam filtering, support-ticket routing, review sentiment and news topic tagging.
prereq: You need 5.1, where text becomes a feature vector of counts or TF-IDF weights.

blocks.text: A bag-of-words vector gives term counts. Multinomial Naive Bayes treats each term in the document as evidence for a class. It asks: which class c makes this document d most likely? The model uses Bayes rule and assumes terms are independent once the class is known.

blocks.where: P(c|d) is the posterior score for class c given document d; P(c) is the prior, the fraction of training documents in class c; P(t|c) is the smoothed probability of term t in class c; the product runs over terms t in d.

count(t,c) is how many times term t occurs in class c; count(c) is the total number of term occurrences in class c; |V| is the vocabulary size; add-one puts 1 in the numerator and |V| in the denominator.

items: Count term occurrences per class and the class priors.
For every term and class, apply add-one smoothing.
Multiply the prior by the smoothed probabilities of terms in the test document.
Take the class with the largest score.
Without smoothing an unseen term gives P(t|c)=0 and kills the whole product.
Many small probabilities underflow, so add log scores: log P(c) + Σ log P(t|c).
The independence assumption is false for real text, but the ranking often works.

blocks.text: Logistic regression is a linear classifier with a probabilistic output. It gives each feature a weight. A positive weight raises the chance of the positive class; a negative weight lowers it. The weighted sum is passed through a sigmoid to keep the output between 0 and 1.

blocks.where: x is the feature vector; w is the weight vector; b is the bias; w·x + b is the linear score z; p is the predicted probability that the label is 1.

blocks.text: L = −Σ<sub>i</sub> [ y<sub>i</sub> log p<sub>i</sub> + (1 − y<sub>i</sub>) log(1 − p<sub>i</sub>) ]
blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> is the true label, 0 or 1; p<sub>i</sub> is the predicted probability for example i; L is cross-entropy loss, lower is better.

blocks.text: For many classes, softmax replaces the sigmoid. It turns class scores into probabilities that sum to 1. Training minimises cross-entropy by gradient descent, often with L2 regularisation to shrink weights.

Prediction uses a threshold, usually 0.5. The decision boundary is linear in the feature space. In text, sparse word counts make this model fast and easy to update. Use the evaluation metrics in 5.3 to compare classifiers.

A support vector machine labels examples with a separating line or hyperplane. For text, a linear SVM is common. It uses labels +1 and −1. The score is w·x+b. The sign gives the predicted class. The SVM wants the score to be at least +1 for the positive class and at most −1 for the negative class, leaving a margin.

blocks.where: y is the true label, +1 or −1; w·x+b is the score; the loss is 0 when the example is correct and outside the margin; otherwise it grows linearly.

blocks.text: Training minimises the sum of hinge losses plus λ||w||². The regularisation term controls overfitting. Only points near or inside the margin, the support vectors, affect the boundary.

The kernel trick replaces x·z with K(x,z)=φ(x)·φ(z). It lets a linear method act in a higher-dimensional space without building φ(x). Text often uses a linear kernel; small datasets may use polynomial or RBF kernels.

Naive Bayes is fastest and works with tiny data. Logistic regression gives calibrated probabilities. Linear SVM often gives strong accuracy on sparse text. All three are baselines before neural models in Unit 6. Some syllabi add decision trees for text; only a few universities examine them. A tree splits on feature thresholds and is not a linear classifier.

figure.caption: Each class multiplies its prior by the smoothed probability of every test word. good never occurs with the negative class, yet add-one gives it 1/5 instead of 0; the positive score 0.08 beats 0.04.

examples.question: Training data: positive = good film; negative = bad film. Vocabulary V = {good, bad, film}. Use multinomial Naive Bayes with add-one smoothing. Test document d = good film. Compute the priors, smoothed likelihoods, class scores and prediction.
steps: |V| = 3. Positive class has 2 term occurrences; negative class has 2 term occurrences.
0.08 > 0.04, so the document is predicted positive.
examples.answer: The positive score is 0.08 and the negative score is 0.04, so the prediction is positive.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
prior = Fraction(1, 2)
p_good_pos = Fraction(2, 5)
p_film_pos = Fraction(2, 5)
pos = prior * p_good_pos * p_film_pos
p_good_neg = Fraction(1, 5)
p_film_neg = Fraction(2, 5)
neg = prior * p_good_neg * p_film_neg
for v in [prior, p_good_pos, p_film_pos, pos, p_good_neg, p_film_neg, neg]:
    print(float(v))

traps: Forgetting Laplace smoothing makes P(good|negative)=0, so the negative score becomes 0 even when other words support it. Add one to every term count and |V| to the denominator.
Multiplying raw probabilities underflows for long documents. Compare log scores; the largest sum of logs wins.
In logistic regression the threshold 0.5 is not a law. A spam filter may choose a different threshold to trade false positives for false negatives.
SVM labels must be +1 and −1 for the hinge formula. Using 0 and 1 in max(0,1−y(w·x+b)) gives the wrong loss.
Naive Bayes independence assumption does not mean words are independent in reality; it is a modelling shortcut, not a data claim.

quiz.q: What does add-one smoothing add to the numerator and denominator in multinomial Naive Bayes?
quiz.a: It adds 1 to each term count in the numerator and |V|, the vocabulary size, to the class term-count denominator.

quiz.q: Why do Naive Bayes implementations sum log probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
quiz.a: A document has many terms, so the product of many small probabilities underflows to zero. Summing logs keeps the comparison stable; the largest log score gives the same class as the largest product.

quiz.q: A positive class has prior 0.5. For test terms, P(good|pos)=0.4 and P(film|pos)=0.4. What is the positive score?
A test document contains a word never seen in the positive class. What happens in Naive Bayes without smoothing, and how does smoothing fix it?
quiz.a: P(word|positive)=0, so the entire positive product is 0 even if other words are strong. Add-one makes the probability 1/(count(pos)+|V|), which is small but nonzero.

quiz.q: What does the sigmoid do in binary logistic regression?
quiz.a: It maps the linear score w·x+b, which can be any real number, to a probability between 0 and 1. Values above 0.5 usually predict class 1.

quiz.q: For a linear SVM, y=+1 and w·x+b=0.5. Compute the hinge loss max(0,1−y(w·x+b)).
Compare Naive Bayes and linear SVM for a very small labelled text set.
quiz.a: Naive Bayes needs only counts and priors, so it trains fast and handles tiny data. Linear SVM needs enough examples to place a margin; with very small data its boundary can be unstable. Naive Bayes is the safer first baseline, SVM often wins with more data.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these classifiers are baselines and fallbacks because they are fast, explainable and cheap to retrain. Modern systems add calibration, class weighting and active learning to handle drift and label scarcity. Search next for multinomial Naive Bayes, log loss, hinge loss, linear SVM, kernel trick and text classification calibration.
